items.title: If you can't test, add a holding dose
items.because: If you can't test today, 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm. That is a holding dose, not a shock: 2 ppm is below what you would swim in, so it cannot over-chlorinate the pool, and it buys a day without pretending to know what the level actually is. Test before adding any more than this.
items.why: ORP is 378 mV and free chlorine wasn't measured, so you don't know what's in the water. This is only for the case where you can't test today. 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine is a holding dose, not a shock, and test before adding any more.
items.how: Start the pump and leave it running, then pour the 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine slowly around the deep end, well away from the skimmer. Keep it out of any bucket that has ever held acid. Leave the pump running afterwards so it disperses instead of sitting in one spot.

items.title: Test free chlorine today
items.because: ORP is 378 mV, well under the 550 mV mark where the water may genuinely not be sanitising. Free chlorine isn't measured -- the ICO can't read it -- so nobody knows whether that is a real chlorine shortage or just the proxy sagging. Salt is out of band, which depresses ORP on its own, so this may resolve once it is fixed. It is still worth a strip test today rather than assuming.
items.why: ORP is 378 mV, well under the 600 mV target, but the ICO can't read free chlorine, so free chlorine is not measured. It could be a real chlorine shortage or just ORP sagging because salt is 987 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band. A strip test today tells you which.
items.how: Take the sample from elbow depth, away from the return jets, and read the strip right away. Write the number down so tomorrow's checklist can use it.

items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 987 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is 987 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band. The cell makes less chlorine below its band and wears out faster, which is likely why ORP is sitting at 378 mV. This is the fix the other items depend on.
items.how: Run the pump and predissolve the 90 lb of salt in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water, a bucket-sized batch at a time. Pour each batch slowly around the deep end. Never dump dry salt on the liner, because undissolved granules bleach and weaken vinyl. Keep the pump running afterwards so it mixes.

dose.label: 90 lb of salt (about 2.25 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Empty the skimmer basket
items.because: Last emptied 5 days ago; the cadence is every 3.
items.why: You last emptied the basket 5 days ago and the cadence is every 3. A full basket restricts flow, and the cell only makes chlorine on water that moves through it.
items.how: Turn the pump off before you pull the basket so you don't get a surge of debris. Dump it, rinse it, and seat it back properly. Then switch the pump back on and confirm it's running.

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 378 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but Salt is out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix that first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP is 378 mV against a 600 mV floor, but salt is also out of band, and ORP depends on all of it. Turning the cell up now only runs it harder against the same problem.
items.how: Do nothing to the cell today. Get the salt in, let the pump circulate for a full day, then read ORP again.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. Salt is out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is already at 100% and running 24 hours a day, so there's no setting left to turn up. Low salt, at 987 ppm, gives it too little to work with. Once salt is in band, the same cell will make more chlorine.
items.how: Leave the cell at 100%. Fix the salt first and see what the cell does with the same settings.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 378 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump runs 24 hours a day, but on a saltwater pool that schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water flows through it. With ORP at 378 mV, cutting hours would cut chlorine production when you need it most.
items.how: Leave the timer exactly as it is. Once ORP is comfortably over 600 and the cell is below full, that's the time to trim hours.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested, so their level is not measured. The target is 50 ppm. A strip test once a season is enough to know where you stand.
items.how: Use a borate strip or test kit on a sample taken from elbow depth. Write the number down. Don't add anything based on this test today.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.
headline: Salt is the problem today: 987 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band
summary: The reading is from this morning. Salt is 987 ppm, far under its band, and ORP is 378 mV against a 600 mV floor. Free chlorine, CYA, TA and borates weren't measured. Start by testing free chlorine and getting salt in, since the cell can't do its job without it.
